newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary telecom Matav IPO talks continue-Ameritech.
newsitem.headline: Hungary telecom Matav IPO talks continue-Ameritech.

text.p: The main shareholders of Hungarian telecommunications company Matav are still engaged in talks on the details of a potential IPO and bourse listing, Matav shareholder Ameritech said on Monday.
Matav chose in January Merrill Lynch as financial adviser and global coordinator for the potential IPO, which according to analysts could be valued as high as $1 billion.

Analysts have said that Matav, which holds a monopoly on national and international long-distance terrestrial telephone communications in Hungary, may sell a stake of up to 17 percent as Hungary's biggest public offering to date.

"Discussions are still going on," Ameritech Chairman and CEO Richard C. Notebaert told a news conference. "We have not made any concrete decisions about the size, the timing, the allocation and the markets.
Matav is 67 percent owned by a 50-50 consortium of Deutsche Telekom and Ameritech Corp, while the state holds a 25 percent stake and the rest is held by a variety of investors.
Matav executive director John Anderson said the consortium has invested $1.7 billion in Matav in the past three years and investments will have totalled $2 billion by the end of 1997.
Notebaert said productivity at Matav improved substantially following the privatisation of the company.

"Prior to the privatisation of Matav, there were 78 (telephone lines) to one (Matav employee)," he said. "Today, three years into the privatisation, that number has improved to 132 to 1 -- and we intend for it to rise to 206 to 1 by the end of 1999."
Ameritech's rating on its core market in the U.S. was 398 to 1, he added.
Matav will continue developments in preparation for when Matav's monopoly right expires at the end of 2001, when the company is likely to face sharp competition, Anderson said.
"It will take another three or four years to make the company competitive against those companies which do not provide full service to all the customers in Hungary," he said.
He added that Matav was preparing for domestic and international bond issues within its debt restructuring programme, to take advantage of lower interest rates.
"We are creating both the first Hungarian bond offering by Matav and our first Eurobond offering."

Matav Treasurer Janos Csak told Reuters that the company repaid outstanding debt and cancelled committed credit lines earlier this year to a total $600 to 700 million and had not decided yet on further steps of the debt restructuring.
"There is a chance of taking up credit, or issuing bonds, but there is nothing concrete yet," he said.
"The main target is cutting financing costs to the minimum and reaching optimal market risks," Csak said, adding that Matav's outstanding debt totalled 130 billion forints.
